extracted.intended_audience: Title IX coordinators, school and college administrators, institutional counsel, HR and compliance staff at K-12 and postsecondary institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of the U.S. Department of Education's final Title IX regulations (effective Aug 1, 2024) and the institutional obligations, procedures, and definitions schools must adopt to comply. Covers both K-12 and postsecondary-specific requirements and procedural changes to grievance, reporting, and supportive-measures processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Definition of Sex Discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations explicitly protect students and employees from all forms of “sex discrimination,” including discrimination based on sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, and gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also prohibits institutions from adopting policies/practices that prevent a person from participating in an institution’s education program or activity consistent with the person’s gender identity. (34 C.F.R. § 106.10.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion from 'Sexual Harassment' to 'Sex-Based Harassment'
rubrics_metrics.description: The new regulations use the term “sex-based harassment” to clarify that Title IX prohibits all harassment based on sex, not just harassment that is sexual in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintains three categories (quid pro quo, hostile environment, specific offenses) but expands the first two categories. (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.10; 106.2.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quid Pro Quo Harassment — Expanded Scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Quid pro quo harassment is no longer limited to employee respondents but includes agents or other persons authorized by the school to provide an aid, benefit, or service under the school’s education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must consider conduct by authorized agents/persons in quid pro quo assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile Environment Standard (Subjective and Objective Totality Test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostile environment is defined as: “Unwelcome sex-based conduct that is sufficiently severe or pervasive that, based on the totality of the circumstances and evaluated subjectively and objectively, denies or limits a person’s ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient’s education program or activity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is broader than the 2020 requirement (which required conduct to be “so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive”). The standard explicitly requires both subjective and objective evaluation of totality of circumstances. (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.10; 106.2.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee Reporting / Notice Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Any employee of a postsecondary institution who “has authority to take corrective action” or who “has responsibility for administrative leadership, teaching, or advising” must notify the Title IX Coordinator when the employee has information about conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All other non-confidential employees must either notify the Title IX Coordinator or provide the Coordinator’s contact information to someone reporting potential sex discrimination. Institutions must include these notification requirements in Title IX training. (34 C.F.R. § 106.44(c).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who May File a Title IX Complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Students, employees, and individuals who suffered conduct that could constitute sex discrimination while they were participating or attempting to participate in the institution’s education program or activity may file complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals may file even if they left the institution’s education program or activity because of the discrimination or for other reasons—removes prior limitation to current participants. (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.2; 106.45(a)(2).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: Educational Program or Activity (Including Some Outside-Conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must address sex-based hostile environment allegations in their education program or activity in the United States, including conduct occurring in buildings owned or controlled by an institutionally recognized student organization or conduct subject to discipline under the institution’s policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must respond even if some alleged conduct occurred outside the institution’s education program or outside the United States. (34 C.F.R. § 106.11.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to Respond: 'Promptly and Effectively'
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must act “promptly and effectively” to end any prohibited sex discrimination, prevent its recurrence, and remedy its effects upon receipt of notice of possible sex discrimination under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This replaces the 2020 “not deliberately indifferent” standard. Complaints may be presented orally or in writing (2020 regs required written formal complaints for investigation). (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.2; 106.44(a),(f).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal Resolution — Voluntary and Limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions may offer an informal resolution process even without a formal complaint, but participation must be voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal resolution is prohibited where the complaint alleges an employee engaged in sex-based harassment of an elementary or secondary school student. (34 C.F.R. § 106.44(k).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive Measures — Purpose and Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must offer supportive measures as appropriate to restore or preserve a person’s access to education programs or provide support during the grievance process; supportive measures are available without a formal complaint or after dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures must be designed to protect safety or the educational environment, cannot be “unreasonably burdensome” to either party, and cannot be imposed for punitive or disciplinary reasons. Parties must have opportunity to seek modification or reversal of decisions to provide, deny, modify, or terminate supportive measures. (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.2; 106.44(g).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual Grievance Procedures (§106.45 and §106.46)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations establish two sets of grievance procedures: §106.45 applies to all complaints of sex discrimination; §106.46 provides additional requirements for sex-based harassment complaints involving a student complainant and/or student respondent at postsecondary institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must follow the procedure set applicable to the parties (general vs. student-specific) and be aware of the additional protections/requirements in §106.46 for student parties. (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.45; 106.46.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance Process — Single-Investigator Model Permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions are once again permitted to use the single investigator model, in which the investigator also serves as the decisionmaker for a single complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using single-investigator, procedures must include a process for assessing credibility through party questioning by the decisionmaker (per §106.46 for student parties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of Proof in Grievance Proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must use the preponderance of the evidence standard of proof unless the institution uses the clear and convincing evidence standard for all other comparable proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an institution applies clear and convincing to other comparable disciplinary proceedings, it may do so for Title IX complaints; otherwise preponderance is required. (34 C.F.R. § 106.45.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal and Appeal Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal is permitted under certain enumerated circumstances, but dismissal is never required; institutions must offer the complainant an opportunity to appeal a dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions are no longer required to offer appeals in cases where neither party are students unless the institution offers appeals for all comparable proceedings (i.e., appeals must be offered consistently across comparable proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 106.46 — Hearing and Cross-Examination Framework for Student Parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations no longer require a live hearing. Institutions using a single-investigator model must include a process for assessing credibility through party questioning by the decisionmaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the postsecondary institution holds a live hearing, it may allow advisor-conducted live cross-examination or allow parties to propose relevant and not otherwise impermissible questions for the decisionmaker/investigator to ask during an individual meeting. If advisor-conducted questioning is permitted and a party lacks an advisor, the institution must provide one free of charge. Note: some jurisdictions may nonetheless require hearings. (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.45; 106.46.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections Against Retaliation (Defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retaliation is defined as “intimidation, threats, coercion, or discrimination against any person by the recipient, a student, or an employee or other person authorized by the recipient to provide aid, benefit, or service ... for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX ... or because the person has reported information, made a complaint, testified, assisted, or participated or refused to participate in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may, however, require employees to participate as witnesses or to assist with an investigation, proceeding, or hearing. (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.2; 106.71(b).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregnancy and Related Conditions — Anti-Discrimination and Reasonable Accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations require institutions to protect students and employees from discrimination based on pregnancy or related conditions and to provide reasonable modifications, reasonable break time for employees for lactation, and lactation space for both students and employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations update parental status definitions to include adoptive parents, stepparents, and legal guardians; employees and the Title IX Coordinator must provide certain information and resources to a student upon learning of the student’s pregnancy or related condition. (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.40; 106.57.)

rubrics_metrics.name: K-12 — Mandatory Employee Notice to Title IX Coordinator
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary and secondary schools must require all non-confidential employees to notify the Title IX Coordinator when the employee has information about conduct that may reasonably constitute sex discrimination under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit K-12 notice obligation mirroring the broader employee-notice rule but applies to elementary/secondary settings. (34 C.F.R. § 106.44(c).)

rubrics_metrics.name: K-12 — Informal Resolution Prohibition for Employee-on-Student Allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal resolution is not permitted where a complaint includes allegations that an employee engaged in sex-based harassment of an elementary or secondary school student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: K-12 institutions must handle such allegations through formal processes; they cannot offer or insist on voluntary informal resolution in these circumstances. (34 C.F.R. § 106.44(k).)

rubrics_metrics.name: K-12 — Inapplicability of §106.46 Student-Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance procedures set forth in Section 106.46 of the regulations do not apply to elementary and secondary schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: K-12 schools must instead follow the applicable procedures (e.g., §106.45/general rules) and comply with other K-12-specific provisions in the regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: K-12 — Students with Disabilities: IEP Consultation Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a complainant or respondent is a student with a disability, the Title IX Coordinator must consult with the student’s Individualized Education Program (IEP) team to determine how to comply with IDEA and Section 504 throughout the recipient’s implementation of grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires coordination between Title IX processes and special-education teams to ensure overlapping federal obligations are met. (34 C.F.R. § 106.44(g).)

rubrics_metrics.name: K-12 — Parental Rights and Confidentiality Exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents of minors may file a complaint with the Title IX Coordinator on their child’s behalf. The regulations allow disclosure of personally identifiable information obtained in Title IX procedures to a parent, guardian, or other authorized legal representative with the legal right to receive disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any disclosure to a parent or guardian must comply with overlapping law, including FERPA. (34 C.F.R. §§ 106.44(j), 106.45(a).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Training Requirement — Incorporate Notification Duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must include the employee notification requirements (who must report or provide contact information to the Title IX Coordinator) as part of Title IX training for employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training should make clear which employees are required to notify and the mechanics for doing so, in order to meet §106.44(c) obligations.
